scenes.title: 마주 섰는데 둘 다 앞모습이 보인다
lines: In a side-view game, two characters facing each other can show us one face and one back. Yet some games keep important poses readable in both directions. We'll examine mirroring, hands and equipment, then see how the pose reads from the play camera. Kula jumps and turns near the right edge of the arena. Follow the direction of her feet separately from the face visible to the camera. First separate rotation from reflection. Turn a person around and their right hand is still their right hand. Reflect the pose in a mirror and the visible relationship between the hands and body reverses. Turning a character around and mirroring its animation are separate operations. We'll put two copies of the same character on our stage. Compare rotating the body with rotating it and mirroring the pose. From one fixed camera, compare how well you can see the face, chest and fist.

scenes.title: 그림의 좌우 반전을 입체 동작으로 옮기기
lines: A sprite can use one drawing reflected horizontally to face the other way. That gives us two directions without drawing both from scratch. In Kula’s jump, the far leg briefly overlaps the nearer one. As they separate, her direction becomes clear again. A 3D character can preserve that same impression, but there is more to check. Mirror a right-handed punch and the other hand takes over. An attached object needs to change attachment points too. Mirror only the body and leave the prop behind, and the action can change meaning. Watch the marked hand and handle to see what must change together. Different equipment on each side makes it more complicated. A sword, shield or one-sided shoulder piece must still fit the character's design after a flip. Link carries a sword and shield in opposite hands. Check what the shield covers when the pose is mirrored. Choose which poses can be mirrored and which need an exception.

scenes.title: 플레이 화면에 맞춘 실제 몸의 방향
lines: The extra work serves the view the player actually sees. If running one way always shows the back, we lose information from the face and front. Showing the needed features in both directions makes the same action easier to read. When Lili changes sides, the gloves and hem stand out. Even in a small picture her guarding arm reads clearly. The body can therefore face at an angle to the direction of travel. A run that looks natural from the side may look angled from a front observer camera. That adjustment serves the gameplay view. Our two synchronized views show the same motion. The floor arrow shows travel and the body's line shows facing. Separating them helps us tell a misaligned model from a pose chosen for readability. Compare the visible and obscured face at normal speed.

scenes.title: 반전을 생각하면 무늬와 글자도 달라진다
lines: Mirroring also affects details beyond movement. When an image flips, lettering on the costume flips with it. A fighter with asymmetrical equipment has different silhouettes at the chest and back. That gives us a reason to check every flip. A vertically symmetric letter can keep its shape through the reflection. Uppercase M and A retain their basic shapes. R reverses direction. In a vertical stack the order stays put, while each letter flips left to right. Compare symmetric and asymmetric letters against the same mirror axis. Pose, props, camera and costume design are linked when a character turns. Mirroring balances production effort with readability. Watch Kula facing the opponent once more. Face, leading hand and feet are the shapes that need to survive the change of direction. The player should be able to see the important information in either direction.
